summary: Josh Snyder introduces PostHog's effort to turn observability data from something engineers read on dashboards into something that automatically submits pull requests. The current workflow is slow: a product signal changes a dashboard metric, an engineer notices hours or days later, investigates, tickets, writes a PR, reviews, and ships. The goal is for a background agent to detect the signal, research the problem, and open a ready-to-review or feature-flagged PR automatically. The pipeline has several stages. Ingestion handles trillions of events per month across diverse sources. A safety-filter LLM classifier drops malicious signals, then signals are normalized with fields for source product, type, content, weight, and embeddings. Grouping clusters related signals into weighted reports; when weight crosses a threshold the report is promoted to a research agent. A critical lesson emerged: off-the-shelf embedding models cluster by structural similarity, so errors land near errors and Slack messages near Slack messages rather than near related signals of other types. The fix is to have an LLM generate queries from each signal and embed those queries instead. The research agent runs the Claude agent SDK in a Modal sandbox with access to PostHog's MCP server for pulling extra data, codebase context, and external MCPs (Linear and Notion). It outputs a problem summary, priority, and a suggested reviewer via git blame. An actionability step routes reports as not actionable, needs human input, or immediately actionable. Error tracking signals are specific and actionable; Slack and session replay signals are generic and harder to act on automatically. If a signal report is too generic, the agent will still attempt a fix, producing noisy PRs, so the system must assess specificity before proceeding. Execution clones the user's repo into a sandbox, runs the Claude agent SDK to build fixes, pushes a PR, and re-runs on CI failures or comments by rehydrating sandbox snapshots, aiming to deliver green PRs by morning. A fourth lesson is that while tokens are not free, experimenting with agents even when expensive is the right approach: running the same problem through an agent 100 times reveals behavioral patterns that can then be collapsed into a cheaper one-shot LLM call or a trained model. The product is currently in alpha with rollout over the coming months. The future vision is a product that builds itself—shipping experiments automatically, measuring impact, approving easy changes via agents behind feature flags, and learning from every PR rejection, deployment issue, or production error resolution to improve the next generated PR.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: PostHog is building a pipeline that converts observability signals into automatic pull requests, collapsing the dashboard-to-PR chain.
Off-the-shelf embedding models cluster signals by structural similarity, not semantic meaning; embed LLM-generated queries about signals instead of the signals themselves.
Error tracking signals are immediately actionable; Slack and session replay signals are generic and harder to turn into useful PRs.
Specificity determines whether the agent produces a useful PR or fixes something at random — generic reports like 'Onboarding is broken' lead to noisy PRs.
Start with agents even when expensive: running the same problem 100 times reveals patterns that can be collapsed into a cheaper one-shot LLM call or trained model.
Evals on representative production data matter far more than local vibe checks for a pipeline handling diverse customer data.
Execution clones the repo, pushes a PR, and rehydrates sandbox snapshots to iterate on CI failures or comments until the PR is green.
Git blame is used to automatically determine who should review the generated PR.
Future vision includes a self-building product: auto-shipping experiments behind feature flags, auto-approving easy changes, and learning from every outcome to improve next PRs.
The product is currently in alpha, rolling out over the next few months.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Josh introduces PostHog and the vision of turning observability data into automatic pull requests instead of dashboards engineers must manually read and interpret. The current process from signal to shipped PR takes hours to days.

sections.title: Pipeline Overview
sections.summary: The pipeline ingests noisy signals, groups them, runs a research agent, assesses actionability, and executes code to ship and iterate on PRs until green.

sections.title: Ingestion and Normalization
sections.summary: Handles trillions of events monthly. An LLM safety classifier drops malicious signals. Signals are normalized with source product, type, content, weight, and embeddings.

sections.title: Grouping and Embedding Lesson
sections.summary: Signals are grouped into weighted reports promoted at a threshold. Off-the-shelf embeddings cluster by structural similarity, so errors group with errors rather than related Slack messages. Fix: embed LLM-generated queries about the signal instead.

sections.title: Research Agent
sections.summary: Runs Claude agent SDK in a Modal sandbox with MCP server, codebase context, and external MCPs (Linear, Notion). Outputs problem summary, priority, and reviewer via git blame.

sections.title: Actionability Assessment
sections.summary: Reports are routed as not actionable (back to pool), needs human input (inbox), or immediately actionable. Error tracking is specific and actionable; Slack and session replay are generic and harder.

sections.title: Execution and PR Iteration
sections.summary: Clones the repo into a sandbox, runs Claude agent SDK to write fixes, pushes a PR, and rehydrates sandbox snapshots on CI failures or comments until the PR is green.

sections.title: Lessons: Evals, Embeddings, Specificity
sections.summary: Evals on representative production data matter; local vibe checks fail. Embed the right representation, not the raw signal. Agents will attempt to fix something even when specificity is low.

sections.title: Lessons: Specificity and Token Cost
sections.summary: Generic signal reports cause agents to fix random things, producing noisy PRs — the system must assess specificity before proceeding. The fourth lesson is that tokens are not free but experimenting with agents even when expensive is correct: running the same problem 100 times reveals patterns that can be collapsed into a cheaper one-shot LLM call or trained model.

sections.title: Current State and Future Vision
sections.summary: The product is in alpha, rolling out over coming months. The future vision is a self-building product that ships experiments automatically, measures impact, approves easy changes via agents behind feature flags, rolls back if needed, and learns from every PR rejection, deployment issue, or production error resolution to improve future PR generation. Encouragement to throw agents at products producing large data volumes.
